title: Working with a bottom set class
author: Jo Castelino
summary: A science teacher preparing for another year of bottom set GCSE classes reflects on how to approach them. She defends setting on practical grounds while recalling how being moved down a set damaged her own confidence as a student. Her central claim is that these classes deserve exactly the same respect, care and high expectations as any other, and that they need more structure, routine, explicit connections between concepts and retrieval practice, not less challenge. She closes by pushing back on the idea that bottom set students are inferior, noting that a weak end-of-topic score is only a snapshot of learning.
points: Setting is defended as a teaching practice because a narrower range of prior knowledge makes it easier to teach and support everyone well.
Bottom set classes need more routine and structure, success experiences, explicit links between concepts and rigorous retrieval practice to build schemas.
High expectations and standards should be identical across sets; the teacher treats all her classes equally.
Lockdown showed that students need a range of resources to draw on, including what is stored in their long term memory.
Calling bottom set students inferior is wrong, since low end-of-topic scores are only a snapshot of learning.
quotes: As a teacher, it is extremely difficult to teach a student who gets tricky concepts such as ionic bonding easily (mostly because they have more prerequisite knowledge stored in their long term memory) while at the same time trying to support another student who cannot even remember what an electron is. In fact, even when we look within a set, we still see a range of prior attainment in the same class but it is a smaller range making it easier to teach and support students well.

When I was at school, I remember being moved to a different class, away from my friends. I did not really understand why until one day it dawned on me that I was in a lower set. This broke my confidence and meant I did worse for some time.
In fact, I treat all my classes equally and still have high expectations and standards for each of them, regardless of set. And I know this is true of many teachers.

With a bottom set class, structure and routine are even more important than with other classes. The students need to experience success in order to feel confident when tackling challenging work. They need help with building schemas through rigorous retrieval practice.

One thing I have learnt during lockdown is how important it is for students to have a range of resources to draw upon when working. These resources are not just physical in the form of textbooks, booklets or core knowledge quizzes, but also include their long term memory.

Bottom set students are not inferior. They may simply struggle to retain knowledge, or they may perform poorly in end of topic assessments (which are only a snapshot of learning at the time). Each of us has struggled with something in our lives and I’m sure we would hate to have been thought of as not good enough.
